item.title: Beyond AI Adoption: People Management, Work Design and Sustainable Performance in AI-Enabled Organisations
item.content:encoded:
AI systems are increasingly used in HR functions such as recruitment, employee analytics, training, performance management and workforce planning. While organizations often expect these systems to improve efficiency and fairness, they raise concerns about transparency, employee wellbeing, job quality and whether such systems genuinely enhance organizational performance. This special issue shifts focus from simply whether organizations adopt AI to how AI-enabled HR systems should be designed, governed and experienced to benefit employees and organizational effectiveness.

The special issue examines the relationship between AI-enabled HR practices and sustainable organizational performance, considering both potential benefits and risks. It invites research exploring when and how AI strengthens or undermines work quality, fairness, employee voice, inclusion and capability development. The collection addresses emerging regulatory interest from bodies like the OECD and EU AI Act, which recognize that AI in employment decisions requires responsible governance.

Appel publié par Journal of Organizational Effectiveness: People and Performance. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • AI-enabled recruitment, selection and fair access to work: How AI screening, automated assessments, candidate ranking, video interviews and people analytics affect fairness, validity, transparency, accessibility and selection outcomes.
  • AI-supported training, development and capability building: How AI-enabled learning systems, skills analytics, career platforms and talent systems affect reskilling, development access, career visibility and employee capability.
  • AI-enabled performance management, monitoring and evaluation: How algorithmic monitoring, datafication and AI-supported appraisal affect fairness, trust, employee agency, wellbeing, reasonable adjustment and performance outcomes.
  • Work design, job quality and employee voice in AI-enabled workplaces: How AI changes autonomy, workload, coordination, meaningful work, participation, consultation and human oversight in people-management decisions.
  • Inclusion, disability, governance and sustainable organisational effectiveness: How organisations design AI-enabled HRM systems that reduce bias, support EDI, protect disabled workers and applicants, strengthen trust and contribute to sustainable organisational performance.

item.title: Green HRM in the Global South: Establishing Sustainability, Responsible Transformations, and Resilient Organizational Development
item.content:encoded:
Green HRM (GHRM) integrates environmental responsibility into HR practices and procedures, enabling organizations to achieve sustainability goals while transforming employees into sustainability advocates. However, most GHRM research originates from the Global North, leaving implementation in the Global South—Latin America, Africa, Asia, and the Middle East—insufficiently studied and scattered across specific contexts.

This gap in scholarship risks producing GHRM frameworks disconnected from the socioeconomic and institutional realities of Global South countries. The special issue seeks to address this by inviting conceptual papers, empirical research, and scholarly discussions that examine how GHRM can advance sustainability, social justice, and economic stability in resource-constrained environments while exploring the unique obstacles and opportunities for GHRM adoption in Global South organizations.

Appel publié par International Journal of Organizational Analysis. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Contextualizing GHRM in the Global South (i.e. the adoption of GHRM, implementation barriers, contribution to sustainability)
  • GHRM and work outcomes in the Global South (i.e. the effect of GHRM on green and non-green individual and organizational outcomes)
  • How GHRM can enhance staff well-being in informal staffing settings (i.e. the relationship between GHRM and workplace happiness, job security, and inclusive practices of staffing, etc.)
  • GHRM in sector-specific context in the Global South (i.e. manufacturing, IT, higher education, hospitality, etc.)
  • National perspectives of GHRM in the Global South (i.e. how GHRM can facilitate effective economic transitions given the frequent scarcity of the resources and climate vulnerability)
  • Leadership, organizational culture, management commitment to sustainable practices (how the aforementioned factors can shape GHRM practices in contexts where pro-environmental values may be nascent)
  • GHRM and Organizational Resilience in the Global South (i.e. why and how GHRM can serve as a tool that contributes to organizational resilience in the light of environmental and operational disruptions)
  • The role of AI and digital transformation in enabling GHRM in the Global South
  • Success stories and case studies of organizations that pioneered the implementation of GHRM in the Global South

item.title: The Startup Workforce
item.content:encoded:
James Bort, DePaul University

Veroniek Collewaert, Vlerick Business School

Yuval Engel, University of Amsterdam

Evy Van Lancker, Ghent University

Johan Wiklund, Syracuse University

The startup workforce represents a distinct and consequential stakeholder in entrepreneurship that has been systematically understudied relative to founders and funders. Early insights from the Stanford Project on Emerging Companies revealed how organizational changes within startups disproportionately impacted long-tenured employees. This pioneering work laid the foundation for understanding how startups differ from established firms in their approach to human capital, including fundamental aspects such as compensation, staffing, and performance management.

Contemporary research has deepened our understanding of the unique dynamics between startups and their employees. Whereas early research identified demographic patterns, illustrating that startup employees tend to be younger and risk-tolerant, recent work has uncovered more nuanced dynamics. For example, experienced employees often join startups when they have partners with stable careers, but can also command wage premiums as firms grow. Startup employees are drawn in by passionate founders, opportunities for greater freedom and responsibility, and the potential for significant financial upside.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Employee motivations and retention across venture stages
  • Recruitment, employer branding, and the role of prior affiliations in startup hiring
  • The influence of early employees on organizational culture, routines, and strategic direction
  • Compensation structures, equity arrangements, and evolving psychological contracts
  • Workforce well-being, occupational stress, and founder-employee emotional spillovers
  • The impact of hybrid and remote work on startup employment dynamics
  • The opportunities and adversity of AI in light of startup employment and work ethic, and workforce diversity, inclusion, and the role of HR professionalization in early-stage ventures
  • Worker voice, collective action, and power asymmetries in startups, including unionization, whistleblowing, hustle culture and exploitation, equity and vesting disputes, and the dark side of founder–employee relations
  • The regulatory and institutional environment of startup employment, including non-compete enforcement, worker classification, equity taxation, and visa regimes
  • Non-standard and hybrid labor forms, including contractors, fractional executives, agencies, platform and ghost work, and globally distributed teams
  • Post-startup career trajectories, including employee mobility, alumni networks, and entrepreneurial spawning after exit, acquisition, or failure
  • The scaleup transition and its workforce implications, including when and how a startup workforce ceases to be one and how HR professionalization reshapes the employment relation
  • AI-native ventures as a new organizational form, where a small number of humans operate agentic systems and the category of workforce is itself reconstituted
  • Startup workforces outside North America and Western Europe, including emerging-economy, informal, and cross-border contexts

item.title: From Human Resource Management (HRM) to Artificial Intelligence Management (AIM)? — Algorithms and the Changing Governance of People at Work
item.content:encoded:
This special issue explores the fundamental shift from traditional Human Resource Management (HRM) to Artificial Intelligence Management (AIM), examining how algorithms are reshaping the governance of people at work. As organizations increasingly deploy algorithmic systems to manage recruitment, performance evaluation, scheduling, and other HR functions, we need to critically understand the implications for workers, organizations, and society.

The collection seeks to bring together diverse perspectives on how algorithms are transforming workplace governance, the mechanisms through which algorithmic management operates, and the consequences for employment relationships, worker agency, and organizational practices. We welcome contributions that examine both the promises and perils of algorithmic management across different sectors, geographies, and worker populations.

item.title: Overqualification and Sustainable Talent Management: Challenges and Opportunities for Human Resource Management
item.content:encoded:
Asta Luksyte, +affiliation not provided in source

Overqualification—when employees possess education, skills, or experience exceeding job requirements—represents a significant and growing challenge in contemporary organizations. This phenomenon has become increasingly prevalent due to economic fluctuations, technological disruption, and shifting labor market dynamics. Despite its prevalence, overqualification remains under-researched in human resource management (HRM) literature, with limited guidance for practitioners navigating its complexities.

The sustainability of talent management practices depends on effectively addressing overqualification to ensure organizational viability, employee well-being, and long-term competitive advantage. Overqualified employees often experience underutilization of their capabilities, which can lead to reduced engagement, increased turnover, and diminished organizational performance. Conversely, organizations that strategically manage overqualified talent may unlock opportunities for innovation, enhanced performance, and sustainable competitive advantage.

item.title: AI Literacy at Work: Implications for Human Resource Management
item.content:encoded:
Maarten Renkema, University of Twente

Laura Lamers, University of Twente

Christoph Lutz, BI Norwegian Business School

Anna B. Holm, Aarhus University

Organizations are rapidly adopting AI technologies, but this creates significant challenges including algorithmic bias and opacity. AI literacy—the knowledge, skills, and attitudes enabling individuals to engage effectively and critically with AI—has become essential for competitive survival and is now mandated by the EU's AI Act. However, research on AI literacy remains focused primarily on educational contexts and individual learners, leaving organizational and HRM perspectives largely unexplored.

This special issue seeks to advance theoretical understanding of AI literacy as an organizational phenomenon rather than merely an individual competency. The editors invite contributions that move beyond both naive enthusiasm and dismissive skepticism, instead adopting critically engaged perspectives grounded in empirical evidence. Contributions should examine AI literacy across multiple organizational levels—individual, team, and organizational—and explore how HRM can facilitate its development and implications for HR functions and practices.

item.title: Addressing Ultra-Low Fertility and Workforce Shrinkage: A Human-Centered HRM Response to the Demographic Crisis
item.content:encoded:
Ingyu Oh, Kansai Gaidai University

Jie Wu, University of Aberdeen

Ho Kwong Kwan, China Europe International Business School

Hyun Jeong Kim, Inha University

Ultra-low fertility, defined as a total fertility rate of 1.3 or lower, is becoming a critical global challenge affecting human resource management across diverse regions including East Asia, Southern and Eastern Europe, and increasingly North America and Oceania. This demographic crisis is transforming HRM into a strategic imperative as organizations face risks of workforce shrinkage, declining productivity, and increased costs for talent acquisition and retention. The crisis requires rethinking foundational HRM frameworks and developing innovative strategies to build sustainable and resilient workforces.

This special issue seeks research that examines how organizations are responding to demographic scarcity through human-centered HRM innovations. It invites scholars to contribute work extending core theories such as the Resource-Based View, Institutional Theory, and Human Capital Theory to address labor market challenges, while exploring practical strategies including expanded parental leave, work-life balance initiatives, AI-enabled workforce planning, and inclusive hiring practices that integrate women, older workers, and immigrants.

item.title: Beyond AI: HRM and the Work of the Future
item.content:encoded:
Sandra Fisher, FH Münster

Janet Marler, University at Albany - SUNY

This special issue examines how artificial intelligence and related technologies are transforming human resource management practices and the future of work. Building on two decades of e-HRM research, the collection seeks to understand how AI differs from previous technological advances, what new capabilities it offers for HRM, and what challenges or limitations need to be addressed. The issue welcomes both papers presented at the 10th e-HRM Conference in Muenster (June 2026) and submissions from researchers unable to attend.

The collection addresses critical questions about which HRM processes should be automated versus augmented through AI, how to mitigate concerns about bias and inequality, and how to maintain human agency and trust in AI-enabled systems. It emphasizes the role of academic research in providing evidence-based guidance on responsible AI implementation in organizations, ensuring benefits for all stakeholders including employees, managers, and organizations.

item.title: Digital Nomadism and the Future of HRM: Rethinking Work, Workforce, and Workplace
item.content:encoded:
Matej Černe, University of Ljubljana

Marko Orel, Prague University of Economics and Business

Fabiola Mancinelli, University of Barcelona

Stefanie Reissner, Durham University

Brian Harney, Dublin City University

Digital nomadism represents location-independent work performed with geographic mobility, raising significant questions for human resource management regarding how organizations manage workers with fluid employment relationships and changing work locations. This special issue seeks scholarship that examines digital nomadism as both a distinctive research context and a lens for reconsidering fundamental HRM concepts in the context of distributed, fragmented, and fluid work arrangements.

The issue addresses a gap in HRM research by bringing together topics often studied separately—remote work, global mobility, platform work, and transnational employment regulation. Contributors are encouraged to develop theory-driven research that demonstrates implications for HRM phenomena, systems, and practices, moving beyond descriptive accounts of digital nomads as a lifestyle group to examine organizational and institutional dimensions.

item.title: Managing the digitally-savvy workforce: Human Resource Management in an evolving digital landscape
item.content:encoded:
Sanjay Singh, University of Dundee

Sateesh Shet, Northumbria University

Tanya Bondarouk, The University of Twente

Paresha Sinha, University of Waikato

James Duggan, Cork University Business School

This special issue addresses how Human Resource Management must evolve to effectively manage a workforce that is digitally fluent, technology-enabled, and deeply embedded in digital ecosystems. As organizations undergo digital transformation, a new type of employee has emerged with distinct expectations around flexibility, autonomy, continuous learning, and meaningful digital interactions. The integration of emerging technologies like AI, machine learning, and HR analytics is reshaping traditional HR functions including recruitment, performance management, and employee development.

The special issue identifies critical gaps in understanding how HRM can strategically align with and support digitally-savvy employees while addressing emerging challenges. Key concerns include digital wellbeing and burnout, ethical surveillance, algorithmic fairness, and digital inequality. The editors seek research that explores workforce planning for digital roles, work design for technology-mediated environments, and HRM frameworks that balance technological innovation with human-centric values.

item.title: The Institutional Fragility of Inclusion in Contemporary HRM Systems
item.content:encoded:
Benjamin Laker, University of Reading

Sven Horak, St. John's University

Toyin Ajibade Adisa, University of East London

Fulya Acikgoz, University of Sussex

While inclusion has become central to human resource management practices globally, its institutional foundations are becoming increasingly unstable. Political and economic shifts, organisational hesitation, and cultural challenges have weakened the norms and mechanisms supporting inclusive HRM. This special issue examines how inclusion becomes performative—publicly supported but weakly implemented—when its institutional backing erodes.

The issue calls for work that moves beyond static views of identity to examine how it is constructed and contested through HRM systems amid institutional uncertainty. Research grounded in intersectionality, social identity theory, and critical perspectives is particularly encouraged, as are comparative studies showing how inclusion operates differently across institutional and cultural contexts. The collection seeks to understand how HRM practices both regulate identity and potentially become sites of resistance and contestation.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: The Interplay of Human Resource Management and Leadership: Alignment, Tensions, and Consequences
item.content:encoded:

This special issue examines the dynamic relationship between human resource management systems and leadership behaviors, addressing how they align, conflict, or substitute for one another in shaping organizational outcomes. The issue recognizes that while HRM and leadership research have traditionally developed as separate streams, they operate interdependently in practice. Understanding their interplay is essential for comprehending how people management actually functions in organizations and for developing more effective, coherent approaches to managing employees.

item.title: Toward a Human-Centered Workplace: Empowering Diversity and Inclusion in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
item.content:encoded:
This Special Issue aims to advance understanding of how AI is reshaping work and employment for underrepresented groups, and to stimulate research on how HRM can foster more inclusive, equitable, and human-centered AI-enabled workplaces. It seeks to bring together multidisciplinary scholarship examining both the opportunities and risks of AI for women, migrants, refugees, older workers, people with disabilities, and Indigenous employees. These aims will be met by inviting conceptual, empirical, and review-based contributions that examine bias, accessibility, trust, human–AI collaboration, inclusive design, and responsible governance in AI-HRM systems. In doing so, the Special Issue will generate new theoretical insights, practical implications, and future research directions that position HRM scholarship to respond more effectively to the challenges and possibilities of AI-driven organizational change, while helping organizations foster more equitable, inclusive, and human-centered human–AI interactions.

Appel publié par Personnel Review. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • AI in Talent Acquisition and Selection: How do AI-based recruitment and selection systems create, reproduce, or mitigate biases against candidates from underrepresented groups (e.g., people with disabilities, older workers, migrants), and what mechanisms can ensure equitable outcomes in AI-assisted hiring?
  • Accessibility and Inclusion in Employment: In what ways can AI technologies be designed to enhance workplace accessibility, enable equitable participation, and expand employment opportunities for employees with disabilities or other marginalized groups?
  • Human–AI Collaboration and Bias Mitigation: How can human oversight, input from minority employees, and inclusive design processes help AI systems learn more equitably—reducing bias and performing more human-like or human-better tasks in HR contexts?
  • Talent Development, Reskilling, and Learning in the Age of AI: How can HRM leverage AI-enabled learning, development, and reskilling systems to support diverse employees and prepare both workers and organizations for ethical AI use? How can organizations use talent development strategies to train both humans and AI systems toward ethical and inclusive performance?
  • Ethical, Legal, and Governance Challenges in AI-HRM: What are the ethical and legal implications of using AI in managing diversity and disability inclusion, and how can organizations establish responsible AI governance frameworks aligned with human rights and DEI principles?
